keyVerseText: And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat. pleasant: Heb. a desire
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word גַּם (gam) is etymologically derived by contraction from an unused root meaning 'to gather,' which suggests a fundamental sense of assembling or adding together. This root idea enriches the common English gloss of 'also' or 'even' by implying not just addition but a bringing together or inclusion of elements. Thus, gam conveys a sense of inclusion and emphasis that goes beyond simple conjunction, highlighting the gathering of ideas or persons into a unified whole.
usageInScripture: With 768 occurrences, גַּם (gam) is a highly versatile adverb in the Hebrew Bible, predominantly translated as 'also,' 'and,' or 'even.' Its frequent use before pronouns and in correlated pairs such as 'both...and' reveals its role in emphasizing addition or inclusion. The range of translations—also, even, yea, moreover, neither, either—demonstrates its flexibility in expressing not only simple addition but also contrast, emphasis, and correspondence within sentences. This variety underscores gam's function as a linguistic tool for linking and intensifying statements.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, גַּם (gam) reminds believers of the comprehensive and inclusive nature of God's work and promises, often emphasizing that blessings, commands, or judgments extend beyond a single subject to others as well. Its root meaning of 'gathering' aligns with the biblical theme of God assembling His people into a covenant community. Furthermore, gam's capacity to highlight addition and emphasis calls attention to the fullness of God's revelation and the completeness of Christ's redemptive work, which includes all who come to faith. Recognizing this word's nuance helps deepen appreciation for the interconnectedness and inclusiveness present throughout Scripture.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 3:6, the phrase 'and gave also unto her husband with her' uses גַּם (gam) to underscore that the woman did not eat the fruit alone but included her husband in the act. This addition heightens the narrative's impact by showing the shared participation in disobedience, emphasizing the communal consequences of sin. The word gam here functions to gather the husband into the event, illustrating the spreading effect of the fall and the interconnectedness of human relationships affected by sin.
